cur:manuscripts-rabbula-virgin-child.summary: Beneath a jewelled arch on slender columns, crowned by peacocks, the Virgin stands on a golden footstool holding the Christ Child, who sits upright on her left arm with a halo of his own. The full-length standing Virgin with the Child, shown frontally like an icon, is one of the earliest such images in a manuscript. The peacocks above were an ancient symbol of immortality.
facts: The Wikipedia list of the manuscript's large miniatures places the Theotokos with the infant Jesus on fol. 1b (1v).

After its time in the Middle East — it was at Maipuc in Lebanon in the 11th century and later at Qannubin — the manuscript reached the Laurentian Library in Florence in the late 15th or early 16th century.

cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-in-.summary: Within a pale green mandorla Christ stands upright, holding a scroll and extending his hand, flanked by angels and by apostles in the sky, above a band of rosettes; on the hillside below stand haloed figures including a crowned empress and an apostle who points upward. The framed, almost icon-like page is one of the most elaborate in the manuscript.
facts: The Paris Gregory was commissioned by Patriarch Photios as a gift for Emperor Basil I between 879 and 883 and is one of the most ambitious Byzantine manuscripts to survive from the generation after Iconoclasm.
Many of its full-page miniatures do not illustrate Gregory's sermons directly but set biblical and historical scenes beside them as a commentary devised for the court.
cur:manuscripts-paris-gregory-christ-in-.notes: Folio derived from the Gallica image sequence (view number minus 13, halved) and checked against folios named on other Commons files of this manuscript; the Commons file name gives the Gallica view number, not the folio. The subject is not certainly identified (possibly connected with the Ascension); the Greek heading is only partly legible in the available image.

cur:monumental-mustair-christ-peter-paul.summary: In the semi-dome of the left side apse, Christ, enthroned and haloed, turns between the apostles Peter and Paul, handing the keys to Peter at the left, while Paul at the right receives a book or scroll; the figures are drawn in warm ochres and reds against a pale ground. The composition echoes the Roman apse type of Christ giving the law and the keys to the chief apostles.
facts: The abbey of Saint John at Müstair, founded c. 780, preserves wall paintings of about 800 arranged in five registers: the life of David at the top, three rows on the youth, ministry and Passion of Christ, and below them scenes of Saint Andrew, joined on the west wall by a Last Judgment.
UNESCO, which inscribed the abbey in 1983, describes them as Switzerland's greatest series of figurative murals, painted around 800.

cur:monumental-mustair-christ-peter-paul.notes: The faded painting may represent a Traditio legis or Traditio clavium; the photographer's description simply calls it Christ between Peter and Paul.

cur:monumental-mustair-last-judgment.summary: Christ sits enthroned in a great circular glory at the centre of the west wall, his hands outstretched, surrounded by angels and rows of haloed figures. One of the earliest monumental Last Judgments to survive in Western Europe, it closes the whole Gospel cycle that runs around the church.

princeton:33998.summary: At the left of this damaged bone plaque Christ stands with long hair and a halo, stretching out his hand toward the girl at the centre, who appears to rise from a couch or bier. The right half of the plaque is darkened and much of the scene is lost. Even in its fragmentary state, it records one of Christ's raisings from the dead, a promise of resurrection.
facts: Princeton records the plaque as Roman or Byzantine, made in Syria or south-eastern Turkey in the 9th–11th century; it measures 7.5 × 7 cm.
It came to the museum in 1994 from Bruce Willsie (Class of 1986) together with the plaque of Christ healing the blind (y1994-75).
princeton:33998.notes: Museum title: 'Raising of daughter of Jairus (Luke 8:41)'. The figure group at the centre is hard to read because of the damage.

walters:W.494.8R.summary: A small framed miniature shows John the Baptist on the riverbank baptising Christ, who stands in the water with his hands joined, beneath a sky of light. The picture sits above a French prayer in verse and is surrounded by a dazzling border cut into lace from the parchment itself. The page comes from the prayer book made for Queen Marie de' Medici.
facts: The lace effect was made by 'canivet', cutting patterns into the parchment with a small knife, an art that first flourished among nuns in France, Germany and the Netherlands.

The Walters describes the book as made for Marie de' Medici while she was regent of France, with 28 miniatures, some of them earlier additions, including nine small miniatures painted in Bruges about 1450.
The manuscript still has its original binding of green and black leather mosaic with gilt pointillé tooling.
walters:W.494.8R.notes: The book is 2nd quarter of the 17th century; the museum does not say whether this particular miniature is one of the 15th-century Bruges additions, so y is set to the book's date. The worklist year (900) was wrong.
